units.text: A person can anticipate seasons without believing there are ‘laws of nature’ in the modern sense. They can build, cultivate and navigate using practical regularities. The history of this concept must therefore not be confused with the history of intelligence. The absence of our vocabulary does not mean an absence of observation, reasoning or technology.

In Physics, Aristotle distinguishes natural things by their having within themselves a principle of motion and rest. A bed is made by an art; a tree develops through its nature. Aristotelian explanation pursues several kinds of ‘why’: material, form, source of change and purpose. These are the four causes, and ‘cause’ here has a broader meaning than the blow setting a ball in motion (Aristotel, Fizica, II) .

This is not a clumsy version of Newtonian mechanics. It is a different distribution of questions. Why does an organism grow in a particular way? What is it made of? What structure characterizes it? What is a part’s function? Contemporary science does not answer all these questions through a single type of explanation, even though it does not adopt Aristotelian physics.

It would be equally wrong to treat Chinese thought as Western physics lacking equations. In Dao De Jing, order is conceived through Dao, relationships, transformations and ways of acting that do not force things. Chapter 25 culminates, in common translations, in the idea that Dao follows what is so of itself, associated with the term ziran. Here we have neither a quantifiable instruction code nor a demonstrated prototype of systems theory. We have a conceptual alternative: order can be imagined without the metaphor of a sovereign issuing commands (Laozi, Dao De Jing, cap. 1, 25, 37) .

The comparison is fruitful if we preserve the difference. We can ask what we gain by conceiving order as spontaneous regularity and what we lose by trying to translate all of nature into obedience. We cannot announce that an ancient text discovered quantum mechanics merely because it uses suggestive words about transformation and relationship.

Another challenge appears in Nāgārjuna’s Indian philosophy. His critique of existence through an independent intrinsic nature, svabhāva, emphasizes dependencies and the difficulty of isolating an absolute foundation. This is not the claim that nothing works or every outcome is possible. The analysis concerns how concepts and things are dependent within a specific philosophical and liberating project. It is not an experimental anticipation of relational physics (Westerhoff, 2026) .

It is nevertheless worth using as a question directed at our own reflexes. When we say an electron ‘has a nature’, do we mean an isolated essence or its behavior in a network of interactions? When we call an object ‘independent’, independent of what exactly? Philosophical comparison can open questions without retroactively granting scientific certificates.

In theological traditions, order and necessity have likewise been separated. Debates about al-Ghazālī show how risky the summary ‘religion denied causality’ is. A central question concerned whether the connection between events is necessary in itself or depends on God. Scholars’ interpretations differ regarding the relationship among occasionalism, secondary causes and his other writings. Challenging the connection’s metaphysical necessity does not simply amount to denying observable sequences (Griffel, „Al-Ghazali”) .

These traditions do not offer the same doctrine in different costumes. Aristotle, Laozi, Nāgārjuna and Islamic theologians discuss partly distinct problems in contexts with different aims. Mixing them into a ‘universal wisdom’ would be as reductive as declaring them mere errors preceding modern science.

The common lesson is more sober: the metaphor of law was not inevitable. We could have organized experience around powers, relationships, rhythms, forms or dependencies. That the language of laws has proved highly productive does not mean all other questions have become meaningless.

This history also has a critical advantage. When someone says ‘the human mind cannot think of nature otherwise’, we can reply: it already has. What remains to be established is not whether alternatives are imaginable, but what they can explain, what they allow us to measure and where they mislead us.
